[[:db/retract 17592186068176 :answer-field/choices 17592186068179] [:db/retract 17592186066832 :answer-field/choices 17592186066834] {:db/id 17592186068763 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4dcf3cdc-27a5-54d1-8c1d-7131e7d4a1a0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068604 :question/problem "What is the result of dividing $\dfrac 3 x$ by $\dfrac {5}{y}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
\dfrac{3}{x} \div \dfrac{5}{y},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac 3 x \div  \dfrac 5 y&=\
		\dfrac 3 x \cdot  \dfrac y 5&=\
		\dfrac {3y} {5x}		
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068597 :question/problem "What is the result of dividing $\dfrac 3 x$ by $\dfrac y {6x^2}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
\dfrac{3}{x} \div \dfrac{y}{6x^2},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\require{cancel}
	\eqalign{
		\dfrac 3 x \div  \dfrac y {6x^2} &=\
		\dfrac 3 x \cdot  \dfrac {6x^2} y &=\
		\dfrac {18x^2} {xy}&=\
		\dfrac {18x^\cancel{2}} {\cancel{x}y}&=\
		\dfrac {18x} {y}&		
	}
$$

Note that in the final step, we canceled out a common factor of $x$ in the numerator and denominator." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068598 :question/problem "Given that $\dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  =x$ and $\dfrac {1+b}{5b^2} =y ,$ then what is $x \div y?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute $x \div y,$ i.e., 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{a}^{2}(1+b)}{3b} & ÷\frac{1+b}{5{b}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\require{cancel}
	\eqalign{
		\dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  \div  \dfrac{1+b}{5b^2}&=\[5pt]
		\dfrac {2a^2(1+b)} {3b}  \cdot  \dfrac {5b^2} {1+b}&=\[5pt]
		\dfrac {2a^2\cancel{(1+b)}} {3\cancel{b}}  \cdot  \dfrac {5b^{\cancel{2}}} {\cancel{1+b}}&=\[5pt]
		\dfrac {10a^2b} {3}  
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068764 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-64ed62a5-f26a-57d4-b199-8c8c51b737ac"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068605 :question/problem "Given that $\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  =x$ and $\dfrac {2a} {14b^2}=y,$ then what is $x \div y?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
\require{cancel}
	\eqalign{

		\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  &\div  \dfrac {2a} {14b^2},
	}
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\require{cancel}
	\eqalign{
		\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  \div  \dfrac {2a} {14b^2}&=\
		\dfrac {2a^3 - 10a} {7b}  \cdot \dfrac {14b^2} {2a}&=\
		\dfrac {2a(a^2 - 5)} {7b}  \cdot  \dfrac {2b \cdot 7b} {2a}&=\
		\dfrac {\cancel{2a}(a^2 - 5)} {\cancel{7b}}  \cdot  \dfrac {2b \cdot \cancel{7b}} {\cancel{2a}}&=\
		\dfrac {2b(a^2 - 5)} 1 &=\
		2a^2b - 10b &
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069503 :question/problem "$\frac{5b}{7}÷\frac{2}{a}=$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

:answer/value "\frac{w+2}{14}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069277 :question/problem "$\frac{12{b}^{2}}{5}÷\frac{36b}{20}=$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
\frac{12{b}^{2}}{5}÷\frac{36b}{20},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12{b}^{2}}{5}÷\frac{36b}{20} & = \\ \frac{12{b}^{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{20}{36b} & = \\ \frac{12b\cdot b}{5}\cdot \frac{5\cdot 4}{12b\cdot 3} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{12b}\cdot b}{\cancel{5}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{5}\cdot 4}{\cancel{12b}\cdot 3} & = \\ \frac{4b}{3} & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186066832 :answer-field/correct 17592186066836 :answer-field/choices ["answer-4dfe5412-1f1d-58e4-94f8-bff7c885cdee"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4dfe5412-1f1d-58e4-94f8-bff7c885cdee" :answer/id #uuid "4dfe5412-1f1d-58e4-94f8-bff7c885cdee" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{b}^{2}}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-64ed62a5-f26a-57d4-b199-8c8c51b737ac" :question/id #uuid "64ed62a5-f26a-57d4-b199-8c8c51b737ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-30011" :question/problem "Given that $\frac{{x}^{2}-64}{x-5}=a$ and $\frac{(x-8)^{2}}{x-5}=b,$ what is $a÷b?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute

$$
a÷b=\frac{{x}^{2}-64}{x-5}÷\frac{(x-8)^{2}}{x-5},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-64}{x-5}÷\frac{(x-8)^{2}}{x-5} & = \\ \frac{{x}^{2}-64}{x-5}\cdot \frac{x-5}{(x-8)^{2}} & = \\ \frac{(x-8)(x+8)}{x-5}\cdot \frac{x-5}{(x-8)(x-8)} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{(x-8)}(x+8)}{\cancel{x-5}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{x-5}}{\cancel{(x-8)}(x-8)} & = \\ (x+8)\cdot \frac{1}{(x-8)} & = \\ \frac{x+8}{x-8}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-03a34a35-604f-5749-8973-20d9e084ced6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-03a34a35-604f-5749-8973-20d9e084ced6" :answer-field/id #uuid "03a34a35-604f-5749-8973-20d9e084ced6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-fec52fe6-cb5d-5c54-b138-3ee0039ec4da" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e9718652-7a2a-51d9-93d2-a20b22cde1b5" "answer-aafbf437-5412-58dc-86e3-6f4bc151f85e" "answer-fec52fe6-cb5d-5c54-b138-3ee0039ec4da" "answer-b1b02b83-478f-5565-a598-0b24437db7e6" "answer-24240d5d-9699-58fb-8663-ef448a1296b2"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e9718652-7a2a-51d9-93d2-a20b22cde1b5" :answer/id #uuid "e9718652-7a2a-51d9-93d2-a20b22cde1b5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aafbf437-5412-58dc-86e3-6f4bc151f85e" :answer/id #uuid "aafbf437-5412-58dc-86e3-6f4bc151f85e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{x-5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fec52fe6-cb5d-5c54-b138-3ee0039ec4da" :answer/id #uuid "fec52fe6-cb5d-5c54-b138-3ee0039ec4da" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{x+8}{x-8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1b02b83-478f-5565-a598-0b24437db7e6" :answer/id #uuid "b1b02b83-478f-5565-a598-0b24437db7e6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{x-5}{x+8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-24240d5d-9699-58fb-8663-ef448a1296b2" :answer/id #uuid "24240d5d-9699-58fb-8663-ef448a1296b2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x+8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069973 :tutorial/content "To divide one rational expression by another, we multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. Just like with fractions!

For example, let's divide $x$ by $\dfrac{3}{y}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x \div \dfrac{3}{y}
$$

To do this, we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. The divisor is $\dfrac{3}{y},$ and to get the reciprocal, we just flip the fraction upside down: $\dfrac{y}{3}.$ Multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x÷\frac{3}{y} & = \\ x\cdot \frac{y}{3} & = \\ \frac{xy}{3} & .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see some more examples!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068967 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083907 :question/problem "Consider the positive infinite geometric sequence that has a first term equal to $18$ and a third term equal to $2.$ What is the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence?" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

From the question statement we have ${a}_{1}=18$ and ${a}_{3}=2.$ We can find the common ratio using the following formula:

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}
$$

Substituting in the known information into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{3-1} & =\frac{2}{18} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{9} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}} \\ r & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have taken the positive square root since we're told that the sequence is positive.

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{18}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{18}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082373 :answer-field/correct 17592186082374 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

For the given geometric series, the first term ${a}_{1}=-10$ and the common ratio is

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-377f3da4-4d13-5ed9-a0c5-00b4eaa5cff5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-377f3da4-4d13-5ed9-a0c5-00b4eaa5cff5" :answer-field/id #uuid "377f3da4-4d13-5ed9-a0c5-00b4eaa5cff5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-98179f33-36bb-5786-aba0-2e8a4ef467fd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-98179f33-36bb-5786-aba0-2e8a4ef467fd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98179f33-36bb-5786-aba0-2e8a4ef467fd" :answer/id #uuid "98179f33-36bb-5786-aba0-2e8a4ef467fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{25}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083279 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b0043402-5216-56a5-82e2-182b3eaa6817" "question-b2fe4d85-a3ec-5968-ad10-7f316b6ab6b7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b0043402-5216-56a5-82e2-182b3eaa6817" :question/id #uuid "b0043402-5216-56a5-82e2-182b3eaa6817" :question/math-academy-id "q-353145" :question/problem "Find the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of the geometric series

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

For the given geometric series, the first term is ${a}_{1}=2.5$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{1.5}{2.5}=0.6.
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{2.5}{1-0.6} \\  & =\frac{2.5}{0.4} \\  & =6.25.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3dfb5c0b-4f43-521c-adf9-750f8155535e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3dfb5c0b-4f43-521c-adf9-750f8155535e" :answer-field/id #uuid "3dfb5c0b-4f43-521c-adf9-750f8155535e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-387e8a10-560d-5d39-9e76-fc3b36e75ef1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-387e8a10-560d-5d39-9e76-fc3b36e75ef1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-387e8a10-560d-5d39-9e76-fc3b36e75ef1" :answer/id #uuid "387e8a10-560d-5d39-9e76-fc3b36e75ef1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b2fe4d85-a3ec-5968-ad10-7f316b6ab6b7" :question/id #uuid "b2fe4d85-a3ec-5968-ad10-7f316b6ab6b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-353150" :question/problem "Find the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of the geometric series

For the given geometric series, the first term is ${a}_{1}=9.6$ and the common ratio is

$$

$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{9.6}{1-(-0.1)} \\  & =\frac{9.6}{1+0.1} \\  & =\frac{9.6}{1.1} \\  & =\frac{960}{110} \\  & =\frac{96}{11}.\end{aligned}

 In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$
{}_{n}{C}_{r}=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

Substituting $n=15$ and $r=2,$ we get

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-209c7809-41c8-59af-ad52-c76253fbc621" :activity/id #uuid "209c7809-41c8-59af-ad52-c76253fbc621" :activity/title "Combinations" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186049434 :activity/course 17592186046647 :activity/steps ["step-1991a9bc-4865-5adb-8f1b-8040622e710d" "step-e0a47519-8739-58a8-b095-6f1943584050" "step-0ff90f75-a9bd-5dc3-8d60-b987f3c76024"] :activity/first-step "step-1991a9bc-4865-5adb-8f1b-8040622e710d" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-1991a9bc-4865-5adb-8f1b-8040622e710d" :step/id #uuid "1991a9bc-4865-5adb-8f1b-8040622e710d" :step/content 17592186083574 :step/next "step-e0a47519-8739-58a8-b095-6f1943584050" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-e0a47519-8739-58a8-b095-6f1943584050" :step/id #uuid "e0a47519-8739-58a8-b095-6f1943584050" :step/content 17592186332939 :step/next "step-0ff90f75-a9bd-5dc3-8d60-b987f3c76024" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-0ff90f75-a9bd-5dc3-8d60-b987f3c76024" :step/id #uuid "0ff90f75-a9bd-5dc3-8d60-b987f3c76024" :step/content 17592186354369 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179677 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aa31a49a-8ce4-5ed7-acd6-a1443ddcc296"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179676 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-59e76c83-715a-52bc-a7bd-8ad37145a622" "question-80763a51-c6ab-5b5d-83cb-358601dd22aa" "question-c384ade7-8329-5b20-a7ce-55cc1c6684d1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-59e76c83-715a-52bc-a7bd-8ad37145a622" :question/id #uuid "59e76c83-715a-52bc-a7bd-8ad37145a622" :question/math-academy-id "q-83971" :question/problem "The rate of growth in the number of people $P(t)$  infected with a certain virus  follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=2P-0.000\,01{P}^{2},
$$

where $t$ is the time, in days, since the virus started spreading. If only one person was infected initially, how many people will have been infected after $5$ days?" :question/worked-solution "A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity. 

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}},
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We start by factoring the given differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{dt} & =2P-0.000\,01{P}^{2} \\  & =0.000\,01P(200\,000-P)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that the constant of proportionality is $k=0.000\,01,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=200\,000.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
P(t)=\frac{200\,000}{1+C{e}^{-(200\,000\cdot 0.000\,01)t}}=\frac{200\,000}{1+C{e}^{-2t}}.
$$

We now substitute the initial condition $P(0)=1$ and solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =1 \\ \frac{200\,000}{1+C{e}^{-2(0)}} & =1 \\ 1+C & =200\,000 \\ C & =199\,999\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(t)=\frac{200\,000}{1+199\,999{e}^{-2t}}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $t=5$ into the expression for $P(t),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(5) & =\frac{200\,000}{1+199\,999{e}^{-2\cdot 5}} \\  & ≈19\,841.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $5$ days, approximately $19\,841$ people have been infected." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "aa31a49a-8ce4-5ed7-acd6-a1443ddcc296" :question/math-academy-id "q-353252" :question/problem "The growth rate of the rabbit population $P(t)$ in a wildlife preserve is jointly proportional to the rabbit population at time $t,$ measured in years, and the difference between the preserve’s carrying capacity and the rabbit population.

Given that the constant of proportionality is $0.0025$ and the carrying capacity is $1200,$ find an expression for the rabbit population after $t$ years, given that there were $200$ rabbits in the preserve initially.

<table align="center">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="right" rowspan="2">
      $P(t)\,=\,\,$
    </td>
<td align="center">
      $1200$
    </td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center">
      $1\,+\,$ {{field-1}}
    </td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Since the rabbit population’s growth rate is *jointly* proportional to the rabbit population at time $t$ and the difference between the carrying capacity and the rabbit population, the rabbit population follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}.
$$

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.0025,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=1200.$ Therefore, the rabbit population growth is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.0025\,P(1200-P).
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{1200}{1+C{e}^{-(1200\cdot 0.0025)t}}=\frac{1200}{1+C{e}^{-3t}}.
$$

We now substitute the initial condition $P(0)=200$ and solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1200}{1+C{e}^{-3\cdot 0}} & =200 \\ 1+C & =\frac{1200}{200} \\ C & =6-1 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(t)=\frac{1200}{1+5{e}^{-3t}}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9ea0a3a4-ab47-57c2-94ec-2bcd3b16dd3c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9ea0a3a4-ab47-57c2-94ec-2bcd3b16dd3c" :answer-field/id #uuid "9ea0a3a4-ab47-57c2-94ec-2bcd3b16dd3c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ea8eee30-c4b3-5768-b0a1-f0b46ef787ca" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ea8eee30-c4b3-5768-b0a1-f0b46ef787ca"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea8eee30-c4b3-5768-b0a1-f0b46ef787ca" :answer/id #uuid "ea8eee30-c4b3-5768-b0a1-f0b46ef787ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5e^{-3t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c384ade7-8329-5b20-a7ce-55cc1c6684d1" :question/id #uuid "c384ade7-8329-5b20-a7ce-55cc1c6684d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-353266" :question/problem "The growth rate of the number of households $P(t)$ participating in a neighborhood composting program is jointly proportional to the number of participating households at time $t,$ measured in years, and the difference between the program’s carrying capacity and the number of participating households. The constant of proportionality is $0.0005$ and the carrying capacity is $800.$

How many households will be participating after $7$ years given that there were $100$ households participating initially? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

After $7$ years, there will be approximately 
{{field-1}} households participating in the program." :question/worked-solution "Since the number of households participating grows at a rate that is *jointly* proportional to the number of households participating at time $t$ and the difference between the carrying capacity and the number of households participating, the number of households participating follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{a}{1+C{e}^{-akt}}.
$$

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.0005,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=800.$ Therefore, the growth is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.0005\,P(800-P).
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
P(t)=\frac{800}{1+C{e}^{-(800\cdot 0.0005)t}}=\frac{800}{1+C{e}^{-0.4t}}.
$$

We now substitute the initial condition $P(0)=100$ and solve for $C.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{800}{1+C{e}^{-0.4(0)}} & =100 \\ 1+C & =8 \\ C & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(t)=\frac{800}{1+7{e}^{-0.4t}}.
$$

Finally, we substitute $t=7$ into the expression for $P(t),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(7) & =\frac{800}{1+7{e}^{-0.4(7)}} \\  & ≈561.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $7$ years, there will be approximately $561$ households participating in the program." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields For example, consider the equation

$$
\log_3(2x-4)=\log_3(x+3).
$$

Since both sides of the equation are represented as logarithms of the same base ($3$), we can exponentiate both sides of the equation by $3.$ This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(2x-4)} & ={3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x+3)} \\ 2x-4 & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4 & =x+3 \\ x & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=7$ is the solution.

**Caution:** Remember that, when solving logarithmic equations, it is sometimes possible to get *extraneous* solutions that don't actually satisfy the original equation. We can't take a logarithm of zero or a negative number.

So, once we've found the solutions, we need to substitute them back into the original equation and check that the arguments of the logarithms are positive. Substituting $x=7$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(2x-4) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{3}⁡(x+3) \\ {log}_{3}⁡(2\cdot 7-4) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{3}⁡(7+3) \\ {log}_{3}⁡(10) & ={log}_{3}⁡(10).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=7$ is a valid solution." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186116523 :tutorial/content "In the previous example, you may have noticed that for the logarithmic equation

$$
\log_3 (2x-4) = \log_3 (x+3),
$$

we were able to "cancel out" the logarithms and equate the arguments:

$$
2x-4 = x+3
$$

This result holds in general. Whenever the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments.

**Caution:** This trick only works when the logarithms have the same base. The equation must take the form

$$
\log_n f(x) = \log_n g(x)
$$

where $n$ is the base of *both* logarithms and $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are the arguments of the logarithms." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115443 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186104428 :answer-field/choices 17592186104432] [:db/retract 17592186104428 :answer-field/choices 17592186104433] [:db/retract 17592186104428 :answer-field/choices 17592186104429] [:db/retract 17592186104428 :answer-field/choices 17592186104430] [:db/retract 17592186104428 :answer-field/choices 17592186104431] {:db/id 17592186106449 :question/problem "Find the $31$st term of an arithmetic sequence given that the $22$nd term is $76$ and the $6$th term is $-4.$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term is given by 

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d,
$$

so we need to figure out the first term ${a}_{1}$ and the common difference $d.$

To find the common difference, we can find the total difference between the terms ${a}_{22}=76$ and ${a}_{6}=-4$ and divide it by the number of jumps, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{22}-{a}_{6}}{22-6} \\  & =\frac{76-(-4)}{22-6} \\  & =\frac{80}{16} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{6}=-4,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{6}$ is $5$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}+5d \\ -4 & ={a}_{1}+5\cdot 5 \\ -4 & ={a}_{1}+25 \\ {a}_{1} & =-29\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-29+(n-1)\cdot 5 \\  & =-34+5n\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can find the $31$st term by substituting $n=31$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31} & =-34+5(31) \\  & =-34+155 \\  & =121\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186104842 :answer-field/correct 17592186104845 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105920 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e16d4c55-4032-51af-b361-3c91c642bb36"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106380 :question/problem "The $10$th and $11$th terms of an arithmetic sequence are $30$ and $33,$ respectively. Determine the formula for the $n$th term of the sequence." :question/worked-solution "The formula for the $n$th term is given by

Since the terms ${a}_{10}=30$ and ${a}_{11}=33$ are consecutive, we can subtract them to find the common difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{11}-{a}_{10} \\  & =33-30 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

Now, we can use one of our known values, say, ${a}_{10}=30,$ to determine the first term of the sequence. Since ${a}_{10}$ is $9$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we have:

So, the formula for the $n$th term of this arithmetic sequence is:

"$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2)(2)) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -2)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the system of linear equations 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{8}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-1}{1}=-1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5ce54675-4c82-511c-b17c-ef8ba86365cd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} #uuid "629a07aa-1bdb-505b-9cdf-8118c6579d3f" :question/math-academy-id "q-136955" :question/problem "Find $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{x+2}{8},\,-2\le x\le 2.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
r(x)={x}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{x+2}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{8}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{4}}{32}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}]}_{-2}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{16}{32}+\frac{8}{12}]-[\frac{16}{32}-\frac{8}{12}] \\  & =\frac{16}{12} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f81fd95e-548c-5041-a689-fc8dd1a4f6b1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-30f439c6-850c-556a-a1db-f9a9d3a4a19c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166645 :question/problem "Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2} \textrm{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\int \dfrac{1}{4-4(x-1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - (x-1)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(x-1)}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|{x-1} \right| >   1.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166806 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-726516a6-793d-5373-8298-c27b8c843f27" "question-6858ad14-b7bc-531f-aa86-afb1603436a5" "question-e0181c3f-486e-569d-aaa1-064715b86f7e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166644 :question/problem "${\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x= }$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 2x)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 - 2\cdot x + 1^2-1^2)\[5pt]
& = -((x-1)^2 - 1) \[5pt]
&= 1 - (x-1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x  = \int  \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt { 1-(x-1)^2 } }	\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166808 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-87c6c320-8ad0-5a7a-8ea7-78e763a7875c" "question-69f3a20c-d1a0-5eb2-90e0-cb5356408eda" "question-fa581feb-4c4c-5d1e-ad5b-763e0315938f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166646 :question/problem "${\displaystyle \int \dfrac{6}{|3x+9|\sqrt{x^2+6x+10}} \textrm{d}x= }$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+10 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+10 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{6}{|3x\!+\!9|\sqrt{x^2\!+\!6x\!+\!10}} \,\textrm{d}x  = \int  \dfrac{6}{3|x\!+\!3|\sqrt {1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2} }	\, \textrm{d}x = {2} \int \dfrac{1}{|x\!+\!3|\sqrt{1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x+3.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}2\int \frac{1}{|x+3|\sqrt{1+(x+3)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+3)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166809 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-42211531-3fd4-52dd-adb0-73d677948d1f" "question-dc07885c-59ca-5761-a1b0-43a8e8cb6e2b" "question-8dc0f52e-b98b-54ec-bcf4-1fa4702113db"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166647 :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\[5pt]
& = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \[5pt]
&= 4 - (x+1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1).$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

*arccosecant*, and *arccotangent*.

For example, let's consider the integral

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{\left(x+3\right)\sqrt{-x^2-6x}} \textrm{d}x.
$$

As it is, this integral doesn't resemble any of the basic integrals we have encountered so far. However, we can complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-6x & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) \\  & =-((x+3)^{2}-9) \\  & =9-(x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of $9$ under the square root, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+3)\sqrt{9-(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{3(x+3)\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This now looks more familiar! Let $u = \dfrac {x+3}{3}.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+3)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-6x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x+3}{3})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x+3}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a basic integral for an inverse reciprocal hyperbolic function, and we can solve it in one step:
$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x+3}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167030 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186203389 :answer-field/choices 17592186203392] [:db/retract 17592186203389 :answer-field/choices 17592186203393] [:db/retract 17592186203389 :answer-field/choices 17592186203391] [:db/retract 17592186203407 :answer-field/choices 17592186203408] [:db/retract 17592186203407 :answer-field/choices 17592186203410] [:db/retract 17592186203407 :answer-field/choices 17592186203411] [:db/retract 17592186203407 :answer-field/choices 17592186203412] {:db/id 17592186204077 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ee17a4e4-1d8d-5373-a5f7-48bfde731f73" "question-67046761-6838-5e5c-bd1f-8e1ae02d3dbf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204576 :question/problem "Consider the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $f(x)={x}^{T}x.$ What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$" :question/worked-solution "The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also write this as

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{T}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203389 :answer-field/correct "answer-ff6fd27f-675e-55fe-8e51-a1443e1cde27" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ff6fd27f-675e-55fe-8e51-a1443e1cde27" "answer-28fad7c5-7710-53c9-96dc-3a22b189fd28" "answer-36ecfad0-45a6-5a26-931b-31fd7b5c023f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff6fd27f-675e-55fe-8e51-a1443e1cde27" :answer/id #uuid "ff6fd27f-675e-55fe-8e51-a1443e1cde27" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{x}^{T}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-28fad7c5-7710-53c9-96dc-3a22b189fd28" :answer/id #uuid "28fad7c5-7710-53c9-96dc-3a22b189fd28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x{x}^{T}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-36ecfad0-45a6-5a26-931b-31fd7b5c023f" :answer/id #uuid "36ecfad0-45a6-5a26-931b-31fd7b5c023f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{x}^{T}x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204579 :question/problem "Consider the function $f,$ defined as

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$" :question/worked-solution "The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

"Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/problem "For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 2(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 44 \\ 18 & 24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203395 :answer-field/correct "answer-4197df66-afcb-5d6f-962d-7c1c812afe7f" :answer-field/choices y(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,f(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

What is 
$\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at 
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}3\cdot 2+1 \\ 3+2\cdot 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & {x}_{3} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 38 & 52 & 34\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5d9e42c8-0cba-572d-9f30-e6b7d5256db3" "answer-field-471955d2-cf1e-544f-a5b9-3b7a749224a4" What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{1} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 13 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

<td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2 & 3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}0-{1}^{3} \\ -1\cdot 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}^{2} & 1 \\ -{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-94b31743-dd24-58bd-b3c9-5a2a72dc5d7a" "answer-field-27e2998c-fb66-52e1-9a0e-14ecb29db474" 17592186373965 :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2u-4v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 0,\,-1\le v\le 5\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+x,\,y+2z,\,x-4y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2u-4v} \\  & =⟨2u-4v+u,\,v+2(2u-4v),\,u-4v⟩ \\  & =⟨3u-4v,\,4u-7v,\,u-4v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-4v,\,4u-7v,\,u-4v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,4,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-4v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-7v)\cdot 4+(u-4v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-6u+8v+16u-28v+u-4v \\  & =11u-24v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+x,\,y+2z,\,x-4y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(11u-24v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{5}(11u-24v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-d9e396d1-f035-59a2-b432-277f6bd182ba" :activity/id #uuid "d9e396d1-f035-59a2-b432-277f6bd182ba" :activity/title "Calculating Flux Through "question-278532bd-d5b2-5391-ac62-5dd37f8bae10" :question/id #uuid "278532bd-d5b2-5391-ac62-5dd37f8bae10" :question/math-academy-id "q-129553" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields #uuid "2c9f2909-7e69-5612-95f1-1f03b540b4de" :question/math-academy-id "q-175591" :question/problem "If $-\frac{x}{12}=-\frac{1}{6},$ then $x=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, let's remove the negative sign from the variable. To do this, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{x}{12} & =-\frac{1}{6} \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{x}{12}) & =(-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{6}) \\ \frac{x}{12} & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}

What percentage of students rode a roller coaster?" :question/worked-solution "We're given a part and a whole, and we must find a percentage. So, we can use the following formula:

$$
\text{percentage}=\text{part}÷\text{whole}
$$

In this case, 

- the part is the number of students who rode a roller coaster, which is $150,$ and

- the whole is the total number of students, which is $500.$

Substituting our numbers into the above formula, we get

$$
\text{percentage}=150÷500=\frac{150}{500}.
$$

To write this as a percentage, we create an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\frac{150}{500}=\frac{150÷5}{500÷5}=\frac{30}{100}
$$

Now we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\frac{30}{100}=30%
$$

Therefore, $30%$ of the students rode a roller coaster." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-41e9ad24-438d-57bd-ba9c-a67eeb3fb7b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-41e9ad24-438d-57bd-ba9c-a67eeb3fb7b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "41e9ad24-438d-57bd-ba9c-a67eeb3fb7b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8bba908b-7b88-591d-9f27-10a6d6474d41" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a4fdf384-ba3c-5858-811d-9e8ebbd7a9d0" "answer-636f630e-1585-5d67-9b3a-b428c2059647" "answer-8bba908b-7b88-591d-9f27-10a6d6474d41" "answer-b9bd8e18-0ed8-549b-baca-f19c0ee012e3" "answer-d4c09eab-8139-5090-a8f7-d565e4fcf770"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4fdf384-ba3c-5858-811d-9e8ebbd7a9d0" :answer/id #uuid "a4fdf384-ba3c-5858-811d-9e8ebbd7a9d0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "15%" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-636f630e-1585-5d67-9b3a-b428c2059647" :answer/id #uuid "636f630e-1585-5d67-9b3a-b428c2059647" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3%" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bba908b-7b88-591d-9f27-10a6d6474d41" :answer/id #uuid "8bba908b-7b88-591d-9f27-10a6d6474d41" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "30%" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9bd8e18-0ed8-549b-baca-f19c0ee012e3" :answer/id #uuid "b9bd8e18-0ed8-549b-baca-f19c0ee012e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5%" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d4c09eab-8139-5090-a8f7-d565e4fcf770" :answer/id #uuid "d4c09eab-8139-5090-a8f7-d565e4fcf770" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "50%" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055465 :question/problem "Evaluate $(-\frac{1}{3})÷((-4)^{3}÷8).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

- To create a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $3:$

$$

$$

- To create a denominator of $20,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator of our fraction by $10:$

$$

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9dd4ab96-7951-5e84-ab6e-c18317468cbb" "answer-field-66177e54-eef7-56db-8506-df97e08453b7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9dd4ab96-7951-5e84-ab6e-c18317468cbb" :answer-field/id #uuid "9dd4ab96-7951-5e84-ab6e-c18317468cbb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-96ef42ad-1530-5d58-820a-ff5c2f14ae67" :answer-field/choices ["answer-96ef42ad-1530-5d58-820a-ff5c2f14ae67"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-96ef42ad-1530-5d58-820a-ff5c2f14ae67" :answer/id #uuid "96ef42ad-1530-5d58-820a-ff5c2f14ae67" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "21" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-66177e54-eef7-56db-8506-df97e08453b7" :answer-field/id #uuid "66177e54-eef7-56db-8506-df97e08453b7" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-463db585-bf6f-5e0d-931b-df42f52effc1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-463db585-bf6f-5e0d-931b-df42f52effc1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-463db585-bf6f-5e0d-931b-df42f52effc1" :answer/id #uuid "463db585-bf6f-5e0d-931b-df42f52effc1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "70" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186138389 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-559e7325-1f2d-5d6d-99bc-9f9ffa4b9d3b" "question-cc1f868e-acd2-53b5-a61f-6b065116ee9a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-559e7325-1f2d-5d6d-99bc-9f9ffa4b9d3b" :question/id #uuid "559e7325-1f2d-5d6d-99bc-9f9ffa4b9d3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-218724" :question/problem "The dimensions of a package in the shape of a rectangular solid are $0.9\,\text{m}\times 0.9\,\text{m}\times 1.2\,\text{m},$ where each dimension was measured to the nearest $0.1\,\text{m}.$ Rounded to the nearest tenth of a cubic meter, what is the upper bound for the volume of the package?

To the nearest tenth of a cubic meter, the upper bound for the volume of the package is
{{field-1}}${\text{m}}^{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "Each dimension is given to the nearest $0.1\,\text{m}.$ So, the greatest possible error of these measurements is

$$
\frac{0.1\,\text{m}}{2}=0.05\,\text{m}.
$$

We wish to find the *upper bound* for the volume of the package. Therefore, we require the *upper bound* of each dimension.

The upper bounds for each dimension are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.9\,\text{m}+0.05\,\text{m}=0.95\,\text{m} \\  & 0.9\,\text{m}+0.05\,\text{m}=0.95\,\text{m} \\  & 1.2\,\text{m}+0.05\,\text{m}=1.25\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the upper bound for the volume of the package is

$$

Remember that a rectangle is a quadrilateral where all angles are right and has two pairs of parallel sides.

- The shape $P$ is an isosceles trapezoid. It has only one pair of parallel sides, not two, therefore, it is not a rectangle.

- The shape $Q$ is a parallelogram. It has no right angles, therefore, it is not a rectangle.

- The shape $R$ is a rhombus. Since it has no right angles, it is not a rectangle.

- The shape $S$ is a rectangle since all its angles are right.

Therefore, shape $S$ is a rectangle. "a327d128-352b-50f9-99e7-ff67c5f44d4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-31996" :question/problem "![](images/13/135ce8e277c0895d36972e12fb7df68447af79765c4acaaba6fb0e63fc498d73.png)

The height of an ice-cream cone is $6\,\text{cm}$ and the radius at the top of the cone is $1.5\,\text{cm}.$ Some ice-cream is leaking from a small hole at the bottom at a rate of $\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.$ If the ice-cream level is $4\,\text{cm}$ at a particular moment, how fast is the ice-cream level decreasing at that moment?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the cone. Let's call $H=6\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cone, and $R=1.5\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the ice cream level. We call $h$ the height of the ice cream in the cone and $r$ the radius of the ice cream top surface. Both of these quantities, and the ice cream volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=4\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of the ice cream:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cone and the ice cream part of the cone must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{1.5}{6} \\ r & =\frac{h}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{4})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{48}\pi {h}^{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{48}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{16}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level in the cone when $h=4\,\text{cm}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\pi  & =\frac{1}{16}\pi ({4}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-1\,\text{cm/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the ice cream is decreasing at a rate of $1\,\text{cm/min}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields A child is tearing the border of a paper party cone-shaped hat in such a way that the volume inside the hat decreases at $10\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The height of the cone is always two times its base radius. At what rate is the radius of the hat decreasing when the radius is $15\,\text{in}?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $h$ the height of the hat and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-10\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=15\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always two times its base diameter. So, we have $h=2r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(2r) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =2\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =2\pi (15)^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ -10 & =450\pi \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{45\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the hat is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{45\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "371ac971-2ba8-5a04-9b8d-bbb2a2347b46" :question/math-academy-id "q-121678" :question/problem "![](images/b1/b18b1e3a686f70a4c583324ddc253e8d334f63f017639bd47f6f483d42582801.png)

An inverted conical dispenser has a diameter of $100\,\text{in}$ and a depth of $110\,\text{in}.$ If a liquid is flowing out of the vertex of container at a rate of $9\,000\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/h}$, how fast is the height of the liquid dropping when the liquid is $60\,\text{in}$ deep?" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=110\,\text{in}$ the height of the container, and $R=\frac{100}{2}=50\,\text{in}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-9\,000\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=60\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{50}{110} \\ r & =\frac{5h}{11}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{5h}{11})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{25}{363}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{25}{363}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{25}{121}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-9\,000\pi  & =\frac{25}{121}\pi (60)^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -9\,000\pi  & =\frac{90\,000}{121}\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-12.1\,\text{in}/\text{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water height is decreasing at a rate of $12.1\,\text{in}/\text{h}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields A conical grain container has a height of $450\,\text{cm}$ and the radius at the bottom of the container is $90\,\text{cm}.$ The container is being emptied so that the distance $h$ from the top of the container to the grain surface increases at a rate of $\frac{25}{3h}\,\text{cm/min}.$ Find the rate at which the volume of the grain is decreasing when the grain level is $180\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The volume of grain is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=450\,\text{cm}$ the height of the conical container, and $R=90\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the bottom. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the grain level. We call $h$ the distance from the top of the container to the surface of the grain, $r$ the radius of the cone at the grain surface, and $v$ the volume of the empty space in the container. All of these quantities change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=\frac{25}{3h}\,\text{cm}/\text{min},
$$

which is positive because the distance from the top of the container to the grain surface increases as the level of the grain in the container decreases. 

We want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when the level of the grain is $180\,\text{cm}.$ At this moment, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =H-180 \\  & =450-180 \\  & =270\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the empty space located between the container's top and the grain surface must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{90}{450} \\ r & =\frac{h}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{5})}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{75}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{75}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{25}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{25}\pi {h}^{2}(\frac{25}{3h}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{3}\pi h\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{3}\pi (270) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =90\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of grain is decreasing at a rate of $90\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-380c73ef-343d-548e-9c09-eeac68deca83"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-380c73ef-343d-548e-9c09-eeac68deca83" :answer-field/id #uuid "380c73ef-343d-548e-9c09-eeac68deca83" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f3225ce6-163f-5ab0-848d-eac7a030fd95" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f3225ce6-163f-5ab0-848d-eac7a030fd95"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f3225ce6-163f-5ab0-848d-eac7a030fd95" :answer/id #uuid "f3225ce6-163f-5ab0-848d-eac7a030fd95" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "90\pi" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a403c1d3-ab4a-51b5-846b-0a043ce7d6fd" :question/id #uuid "a403c1d3-ab4a-51b5-846b-0a043ce7d6fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-359420" :question/problem "![](images/ff/ffdfbbfcbc2a01e79fd9490f05744b2d0bf1d24dd616a0b318ee95acfa26e9ba.png)

A cone-shaped pile of salt is being depleted so that the volume of the pile decreases at $5\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{hr}.$ The height of the pile is always one-half of its base diameter. Find the rate of the pile’s height decrease when the height is $5\,\text{m}.$ Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The height is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} $\text{m}/\text{hr}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $h$ the height of the pile and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-5\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{hr},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=5\,\text{m}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the height is always one-half of its base diameter. So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{1}{2}d \\ h & =\frac{1}{2}(2r) \\ r & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi (h)^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\  & =\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\pi  & =\pi (5)^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -5\pi  & =25\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{5}\,\text{m}/\text{hr}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the pile is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{5}\,\text{m}/\text{hr}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$

![](images/b9/b974b6e782801fbe2099971afd0df9a5c6e05a10afc2ce0e4054c850088e753b.png)

The formula for the volume $V$ of a cube with sides of length $s$ is given by

$$

So the volume of the cube is $8\,\textrm{cm}^3.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110837 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186175186 :answer-field/choices 17592186175188] [:db/retract 17592186175186 :answer-field/choices 17592186175189] [:db/retract 17592186175186 :answer-field/choices 17592186175190] [:db/retract 17592186175198 :answer-field/choices 17592186175200] [:db/retract 17592186175198 :answer-field/choices 17592186175203] {:db/id 17592186175950 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9b70f694-75c4-56a5-8060-3f93ae37aa40" "question-c45730a9-37f0-5369-8e28-cf166dacf491" "question-2f5058c8-bee4-550a-9863-d36cd2227082"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175806 :question/problem "What is the sum of the series $\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{(\pi/3)^3}{3!} + \dfrac{(\pi/3)^5}{5!}-\cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n}(\pi/3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+\cdots\,?$" :question/worked-solution "We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \sin x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{(\pi /3)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /3)^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯ \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{(\pi /3)^{3}}{3!}+\frac{(\pi /3)^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(\pi /3)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175951 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-38c8627e-3005-599a-a37a-fb4e0aa52cad" "question-3922f3d0-9ec0-55ed-b2ff-7790813baa5b" "question-b939d5df-d459-5fd4-9292-d3dcc1c6afac" "question-b2664ee6-8acb-52ad-889d-ed63a283e637" "question-6b7d68eb-3099-57db-9579-cc9c26274e37"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175807 :question/problem "Find the sum $1 - \dfrac{9}{2!} + \dfrac{81}{4!}-\cdots + \dfrac{(-1)^{n}3^{2n}}{(2n)!} \,\cdots \,.$" :question/worked-solution "We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x) = \cos x.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1-\frac{1}{2!}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{4!}{x}^{4}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}\,{x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=3$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3) & =1-\frac{{3}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{3}^{4}}{4!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{3}^{2n}}{(2n)!}\,⋯ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(3) & =1-\frac{9}{2!}+\frac{81}{4!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{3}^{2n}}{(2n)!}\,⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\cos(3).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176508 :question/problem "What is the sum of the series $-2+\frac{8}{3!}-\frac{32}{5!}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}(-2)^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\,?$" :question/worked-solution "We recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}{x}^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-2$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
