where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $y=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "167e09bf-7031-5c07-aef8-581424ee1431"} {:db/id 17592186497442 :step/content {:db/id 17592186345245 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cee7c2d-32de-5ecb-b754-ad79568f9d67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186342741} {:answer/id #uuid "5fee99df-a2f2-53ad-aa42-aeb2b8227900" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186343052} {:answer/id #uuid "7d9b8c0d-eb50-5a20-b648-4799432e59b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186343321} {:answer/id #uuid "817d31a5-4314-5a33-8e83-382ed5fd5388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186343350} {:answer/id #uuid "8d7f6c1c-7a72-538c-9708-f7cf3bcb5c66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186343475}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343475} :answer-field/id #uuid "946d4e0c-fe04-5d7a-bb82-af9edb848223" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344748}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a681b3bc-0951-5b58-83e9-55d23d5a0373" :question/math-academy-id "q-76688" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "61e4b9a7-6a75-55d9-96ed-a67877cbb8d8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497424}} {:db/id 17592186497450 :step/content {:db/id 17592186345237 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12b1571f-f5f7-562d-80a0-607aa3516530" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186342403} {:answer/id #uuid "4c9c1e54-997f-58a0-bd84-3b903059ab31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (3-{cos}^{6}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186342870} {:answer/id #uuid "7da69662-1fe5-58e3-b0c0-5897eb5c94d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186343322} {:answer/id #uuid "cfd26a22-60c5-5518-ab97-c388fe07fef6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186344065} {:answer/id #uuid "d1097377-be4e-5b0d-8118-afb24f1f0f9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186344076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343322} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d5e348e-6403-58e5-a33c-30c8b85d2e1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d123bbf4-7b8c-5b08-b206-9ffde691a39b" :question/math-academy-id "q-76610" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}

$$

and therefore

$$

$$

$$

$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}

and therefore

$$

$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

form by $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le 0.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{4}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{0}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}{|}_{-\pi /4}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "007eb044-32d9-58ff-9c52-c7f147890537" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531697}} {:db/id 17592186531697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186364413 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "49adc8e9-1dc5-5cb5-9175-f91e269efe35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192" :db/id 17592186364415} {:answer/id #uuid "e94aff50-1cf2-58b3-85e2-e76471a133a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186364416} {:answer/id #uuid "7fdf46cb-8dea-538a-974a-83bf0db567f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "256" :db/id 17592186364417} {:answer/id #uuid "119dacc9-0e3b-5285-87d0-21d3cc26e860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "512" :db/id 17592186364418} {:answer/id #uuid "bddd3fe2-39af-5dc8-a534-e22068d4a73c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "384" :db/id 17592186364419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186364415} :answer-field/id #uuid "7944764b-8f2e-517b-9311-deccaafc6156" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186364414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "13c81ebd-eba4-55aa-a40f-bfa1b49cc9df" :question/math-academy-id "q-76763" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}y$ along the polar curve $r=4$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\pi -0}{4}-\frac{0-0}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}

$0\le \theta \le \pi ?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ))}^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "eb57df81-a928-539a-b8d1-a80b4295d9a1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186531699}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "082112eb-8a26-5265-b137-26bd8c295b06" :answer/type {:db/id :topic/id #uuid "99a15aac-d6e4-5b90-ad24-876fee287562" :topic/math-academy-id 5868} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205190 :tutorial/content "Consider the multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n \to\mathbb R,$ defined by

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n,$ defined by

![](images/af/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](images/14/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

In the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "17350522-fdcb-5adf-a0e3-30fbe076474e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12384 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "55b69b88-94a5-5e68-b80c-fdb21b7034b5" :step/math-academy-id 610762 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205056}} {:db/id 17592186205056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205191 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be two differentiable vector-valued functions. We want to compute the derivative of the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}))$ with respect to $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

The **chain rule for total derivatives** tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{m \times n}
=
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Here, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.

**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} = 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\qquad \text{(WRONG!)}
$$

This is incorrect because the inner matrix dimensions do not agree, making it an invalid matrix product.

Let's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "be71f9c1-7d65-5804-9536-88b35b9f95f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12385 :tutorial/title "The Chain Rule for Total Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "c4066bbf-680a-5ee8-9250-732582cd85b8" :step/math-academy-id 610763 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205057}} {:db/id 17592186205057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205198 :tutorial/content "Suppose we define
![](images/11/11259475d7bcdbbdf2d28e6540f1af92282a188d05dd6d70038b00ec5ab611a5.svg)

Then, we have $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2.$ 

Let's see how to compute the derivative for the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})).$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} 
= \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}
\cdot
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is also a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Computing our derivatives, we get
![](images/91/918c4e1af2c1f33f6d056843ee0d038b4b91dc67e8c112c899a05c273d5fcd89.svg)

Then, by the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

:step/math-academy-id 610771 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205061}} {:db/id 17592186205061 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205199 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following differentiable functions:

$$
\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p, \qquad

\mathbf{z}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^q, \qquad \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^m
$$

The chain rule can be extended in the natural way as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) 
= 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z}}_{m\times q} 
\cdot 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y}}_{q\times p} 
\cdot 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}}_{p\times n}
$$

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "7e23add8-cf11-5e3b-9950-84e432ab21da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13109 :tutorial/title "Extending the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "b82af8bd-d320-54be-9e80-1c9573305b84" :step/math-academy-id 610774 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205062}} {:db/id 17592186205062 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204101 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203870 :question/id #uuid "1fb3c5e6-ead1-52be-aa8c-3543e69bac24" :question/math-academy-id "e-17950"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "12de0411-fa8a-5be0-9d80-3e174cf92707" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204577} {:db/id 17592186204591} {:db/id 17592186531566} {:db/id 17592186531614} {:db/id 17592186531620} {:db/id 17592186531633} {:db/id 17592186531637}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating the Composition of Three Functions"} :step/id #uuid "6c01f312-b060-5ffd-9c41-09f2f766fdf7" :step/math-academy-id 610775} {:db/id 17592186205064 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205217 :tutorial/content "Let's *verify* that our result from the previous slide is correct by computing the derivative directly.

Recall that
![](images/3e/3e421d8e8fdac73c75fbec18f98a7b338ac46083ea0c4d07cd8f07121420dac1.svg)

First, we substitute $\mathbf{y}$ into $\mathbf{f}$ to write $\mathbf{f}$ explicitly in terms of $\mathbf{x}{:}$
![](images/58/58f11371168007d979c4ffeae1e6643441459b015d7cf7a08e60c5b05e4f93a1.svg) 

Now, we compute the derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $\mathbf x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This agrees with the result we obtained using the chain rule." :tutorial/id #uuid "06ee1fff-0a96-5071-a12d-9ca9bb198db8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14943 :tutorial/title "Verifying the Chain Rule Example"} :step/id #uuid "1fde6146-c615-51c0-a7cd-e09772b86108" :step/math-academy-id 610802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205058}} {:db/id 17592186205065 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205218 :tutorial/content "We can use the chain rule for functions that use matrices in their definition.

For example, consider the functions $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{y},$ where $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^2,$ and the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are given by
![](images/c7/c721b41403d149ac6d97e543aabb22dec2ce200c99e4dccdae09204eb520b555.svg)
What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = [2, \, 0, \, -1]^T?$

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Since these derivatives are constant matrices, the value at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is simply their product. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & 14 \\ 2 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f342078-4ed2-5d64-9c73-2ad6cd06661f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14944 :tutorial/title "The Chain Rule for Functions Defined Using Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "bf30b4c4-d817-5a30-8671-ae1a5b55d2c3" :step/math-academy-id 610803 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205060}}] :activity/title "The Chain Rule for Total Derivatives" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204181} {:db/id 17592186205055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205190 :tutorial/content "Consider the multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n \to\mathbb R,$ defined by

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n,$ defined by

![](images/af/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](images/14/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

In the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "17350522-fdcb-5adf-a0e3-30fbe076474e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12384 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "55b69b88-94a5-5e68-b80c-fdb21b7034b5" :step/math-academy-id 610762 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205056}} {:db/id 17592186205190 :tutorial/content "Consider the multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n \to\mathbb R,$ defined by

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n,$ defined by

![](images/af/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](images/14/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

In the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "17350522-fdcb-5adf-a0e3-30fbe076474e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12384 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186205056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205191 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be two differentiable vector-valued functions. We want to compute the derivative of the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}))$ with respect to $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

The **chain rule for total derivatives** tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{m \times n}
=
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Here, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.

**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} = 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\qquad \text{(WRONG!)}
$$

This is incorrect because the inner matrix dimensions do not agree, making it an invalid matrix product.

\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Since these derivatives are constant matrices, the value at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is simply their product. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & 14 \\ 2 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f342078-4ed2-5d64-9c73-2ad6cd06661f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14944 :tutorial/title "The Chain Rule for Functions Defined Using Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "bf30b4c4-d817-5a30-8671-ae1a5b55d2c3" :step/math-academy-id 610803 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205060}} {:db/id 17592186205060 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204100 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203873 :question/id #uuid "2d9c4fa9-4d6a-5b0f-905d-0795fb26e9bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-18032"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fc95d2b5-9318-58b0-aa61-963954bf4594" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204582} {:db/id 17592186204590} {:db/id 17592186531563} {:db/id 17592186531600} {:db/id 17592186531627}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating Functions Defined Using Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "0a1a3945-b507-5d6d-b827-7b3f410bd223" :step/math-academy-id 610771 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205061}} {:db/id 17592186205061 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205199 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following differentiable functions:

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278509 :question/id #uuid "d5fb8cb6-33d1-582b-8cf3-53ceebac82e8" :question/math-academy-id "q-161435"} {:db/id 17592186278522 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 4$ and $-2\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-2}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u+v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,-2\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u+v} \\  & =⟨u+v-v,\,2v-(u+v),\,uv⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\,v-u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u,\,v-u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-1)+(v-u)\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-u-v+u+uv \\  & =uv-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(uv-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-2}^{3}uv-v\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198610 :question/id #uuid "a3bcb9d3-050c-5ab9-bd2a-436465223147" :question/math-academy-id "q-161360" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f754a120-8886-56d3-b535-398f13b91c9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398529} {:answer/id #uuid "d28df103-ae23-5647-a506-1bc60c332868" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}+uv+{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398530} {:answer/id #uuid "e85142cb-e059-512c-8b7b-18eee7a8c253" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2uv" :db/id 17592186398531} {:answer/id #uuid "e433762d-59a0-5efb-bef2-7687d8583f2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}" :db/id 17592186398532} {:answer/id #uuid "3a53a3c7-e2f5-50e9-afd4-d3b986017cf4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2(u+v)^{2}" :db/id 17592186398533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398531} :answer-field/id #uuid "185487e5-090f-5815-93b2-dfc0c983e691" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398528}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u+v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u+v} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2},\,(u+v)^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot (-1)+{v}^{2}\cdot (-1)+(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}+2uv+{v}^{2} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2},\,{y}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278495 :question/id #uuid "0bf481ef-95d3-5b3f-b324-29ecd57febda" :question/math-academy-id "q-161358" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10279bac-75c2-5820-bf33-84359cbf720e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7u+4v" :db/id 17592186275617} {:answer/id #uuid "397e53f3-63a0-518a-999e-8c3d8631bb27" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4u+7v" :db/id 17592186275987} {:answer/id #uuid "897e0260-ef83-5fe5-9ee2-95ed9d4cd1a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7u+8v" :db/id 17592186276718} {:answer/id #uuid "bd3f2f9b-ef08-5972-b94d-02717ccd84df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8u-7v" :db/id 17592186277162} {:answer/id #uuid "ee6d4a87-66ae-58b1-806a-631ade59590d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-7u-8v" :db/id 17592186277571}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275617} :answer-field/id #uuid "8692e3d1-c9bd-5cca-9274-6af9e13d6963" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277965}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=3x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 5$ and $-3\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,3u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-3\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,3⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,-y,\,2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-2v,\,-v,\,2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186278510 :question/id #uuid "279f5fbf-fc31-5667-8b25-7d1c25dc2d02" :question/math-academy-id "q-161441" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10b5412c-a9ab-5d1e-8d26-9a4c8f27c8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+7v" :db/id 17592186275625} {:answer/id #uuid "16ffd34a-40d1-5df6-87ca-5595406b5509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4u+v" :db/id 17592186275691} {:answer/id #uuid "85617ab2-8072-5a8d-9456-259cf0bef230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4v-u" :db/id 17592186276672} {:answer/id #uuid "ce5a4f92-85cc-5237-ba98-a4e395360811" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2u+v" :db/id 17592186277305} {:answer/id #uuid "fe69b9d6-2d90-53f7-90a8-f4819b62096e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2u+4v" :db/id 17592186277710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275625} :answer-field/id #uuid "7a3b6104-863d-512e-9bea-c3b626c9b6e0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277943}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y-z,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423120 :question/id #uuid "29805411-7a4c-51f7-893d-a0f3dc3cef10" :question/math-academy-id "q-161377"} {:db/id 17592186423123 :question/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,v-u⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,-3\le v\le 0\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=v-u} \\  & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1+(u-v)^{2}\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =5uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}5uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423124 :question/id #uuid "ef91d27f-5ce3-5c48-b5b9-4ec732b3b2e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-161471" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198389 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a3486150-b3c2-5faf-99d5-b42ced350996" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "556660a7-ba40-5142-a23c-96cdb3bb38b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8u-23v" :db/id 17592186423090} {:answer/id #uuid "86aaa33f-073f-5b9c-b6ed-02e42f1370d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "12u-v" :db/id 17592186423099} {:answer/id #uuid "8fa80cac-9ed0-54f2-a0fb-a71697486081" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8u+14v" :db/id 17592186423101} {:answer/id #uuid "9d9623af-3bba-5a0d-9c01-61a215703653" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5u-17v" :db/id 17592186423103} {:answer/id #uuid "b721d1da-8cb3-5423-bdff-f515271a77db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "u-6v" :db/id 17592186423105}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "9d9623af-3bba-5a0d-9c01-61a215703653" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5u-17v" :db/id 17592186423103} :answer-field/id #uuid "de6e4169-2fd0-5a0b-b7fe-172964aca58f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186423119}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-3y$ for $-1\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$

$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩ \\  & =(2u-3v)\cdot (-1)+(2u-6v)\cdot (3)+(u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+3v+6u-18v+u-2v \\  & =5u-17v.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z=g(x,y),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,y)=⟨x,\,y,\,g(x,y)⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186423121 :question/id #uuid "431ed508-ca53-50c3-b7a4-875fc9b23084" :question/math-academy-id "q-161449"} {:db/id 17592186423122 :question/id #uuid "4ec0f874-f1a4-5c03-8a41-bf094ee7ee97" :step/math-academy-id 44446 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199282}} {:db/id 17592186199300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199470 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "d20203b0-e15f-5061-ae68-16676ec933dc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7653 :tutorial/title "Formulas for Flux Over Cartesian Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "299c6f48-c761-519a-8d96-161fea9d6df0" :step/math-academy-id 44449 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199299}} {:db/id 17592186199306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199473 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left\langle (x-y)^2, \:(x+y)^2, \: 12xy \right\rangle
$$

 

through the surface $S$ defined by the Cartesian equation 

$$
z=2y-2x
$$

for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$ 

For surfaces like this, substituting $x=u$ and $y=v,$ we obtain a parametrization 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: 2v-2u \right\rangle
$$

over the domain 

$$
D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 1, \: 0 \leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

 

Recall that for a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v-2u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨(x-y)^{2},\,(x+y)^{2},\,12xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2v-2u} \\  & =⟨(u-v)^{2},\,(u+v)^{2},\,12uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)^{2},\,(u+v)^{2},\,12uv⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)^{2}\cdot 2+(u+v)^{2}\cdot (-2)+12uv\cdot 1 \\  & =4uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x-y)^{2},\,(x+y)^{2},\,12xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}4uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =[{u}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =({1}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot ({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f32d6993-cd62-5fe7-98f3-9a89a815dbfc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7666 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "dd32837c-4771-57ff-abbc-360334e17eeb" :step/math-academy-id 44522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199295}}] :activity/title "Calculating Flux Through Cartesian Surfaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198485} {:db/id 17592186199306 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199473 :tutorial/content "Let's calculate the flux of the vector field
